content: The extent to which the HIV status of tuberculosis (TB) patients is determined is critical, as it allows for appropriate linkage to HIV services. This process evaluates the effectiveness of programs in promoting HIV testing, which serves as both a prevention tool and an entry point for early care and treatment, particularly for high-risk populations. Targets for the percentage of key populations who know their HIV status should exceed those set for the general population. It assesses whether individuals starting ART within the past 12 months underwent a retest to verify their HIV diagnosis. Surveys also assess the willingness of individuals to use home-based self-testing kits, providing insights into the accessibility and acceptability of this testing method. This indicator is particularly relevant in generalized epidemics, where broad-based testing efforts are essential. It also evaluates the program's ability to identify and test the sexual partners of people living with HIV, aiming to prevent ongoing transmission in serodiscordant couples and to enroll HIV-positive partners in care services. These activities address clinical HIV program processes and outcomes, ensuring the availability of diagnostic tests and reagents without stock-outs. Laboratory capacity for HIV testing is also monitored, focusing on the number of facilities capable of performing clinical laboratory tests and their performance in external quality assurance (EQA) programs. Linkage, enrollment, and retention in HIV care are essential components of the HIV care cascade. Linking individuals who test HIV-positive to prevention, treatment, and care services is critical to realizing the full benefits of knowing one’s HIV status. Programs must invest significant effort in ensuring that individuals diagnosed with HIV are promptly enrolled in care and retained over time. This includes addressing co-infections such as tuberculosis (TB) and providing comprehensive services like nutritional and social support. Retention in pre-ART care is particularly challenging due to high attrition and mortality rates. Monitoring pre-ART retention is important in settings where this is an issue. This indicator tracks progress in increasing the proportion of individuals in care and identifies gaps in service delivery. Enrollment in care begins when an HIV-positive individual presents at a facility and a patient file is opened. Retention in care refers to patients routinely attending services as needed, excluding those who have died or been lost to follow-up. For key populations, monitoring linkage, enrollment, and retention in care is particularly important due to their higher disease burden and greater difficulty accessing services. HIV-associated tuberculosis remains a leading cause of death among people living with HIV. Collaborative TB/HIV activities are essential to reduce mortality, with early ART initiation being a critical component. Recent developments, such as the use of Xpert MTB/RIF for rapid TB diagnosis, have improved the detection and management of TB among people living with HIV. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of collaborative TB/HIV activities require data from both TB and HIV programs, which often use different databases and reporting systems. This can lead to inconsistencies in reported data. Efforts must focus on improving data collection, ensuring complete reporting of both numerators and denominators, and addressing gaps in coverage indicators such as isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). In summary, effective HIV and TB care requires robust systems for testing, linkage, enrollment, and retention in care. Programs must address challenges in data collection, service delivery, and patient management to improve outcomes and reduce mortality among people living with HIV and TB.
